summary: The former Marine Corps Air Station Tustin — decommissioned in 1999 — left behind two colossal blimp hangars, each roughly 17 stories tall and over 1,000 feet long, now towering over a massive redevelopment that is reshaping the city's southeastern quadrant into a mixed-use district with parks, housing, and retail. That single fact captures Tustin's strange duality: it reads as a quiet, flat Orange County suburb at 7,158 people per square mile, yet it sits on one of the most ambitious infill projects in Southern California. The median home price of $890,600 against a median household income of $108,435 yields a price-to-income ratio above 8:1, meaning even at the local median income, buying requires substantial savings or dual incomes; renting at $2,340 per month consumes roughly 26% of that gross income, a more manageable ratio. Daily highs averaging 75°F with 9.3 hours of sunshine make the climate genuinely mild year-round — warm but buffered from inland heat by Tustin's position a few miles from the Santa Ana Mountains' western foothills. Major employers in surrounding Irvine, Santa Ana, and along the I-5/405 corridors in aerospace, healthcare, and tech mean job switching rarely requires relocating, though freeway commutes are the norm. Tustin is a place where Cold War-era infrastructure is literally being converted into a new downtown — whether that transformation outpaces its housing costs is the central question.
